questions.question: A student hooks a spring scale onto a brick and drags it across the classroom floor, watching the spring inside it stretch. What does the spring scale measure?
questions.answer: How hard she pulls on the brick
choices: How hard she pulls on the brick
How much matter is in the brick
How fast the brick slides along
How far the brick slides along
questions.context: A spring scale measures force: the harder the pull, the farther its spring stretches, and the pointer reads the force in newtons. The amount of matter in the brick is its mass, which a balance measures, and the brick's speed and distance need a timer and a metre stick.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.1D puts scales among the 5th grader's tools, and 5th-grade force lessons use a spring scale to measure a pull in newtons.

questions.question: A student pours water into a graduated cylinder to measure its volume in millilitres. Up close, the water's surface is not flat: it curves down in the middle, like a shallow bowl. Where should she read the level?
questions.answer: The bottom of the curve, seen at eye level
choices: The bottom of the curve, seen at eye level
The top of the curve, seen at eye level
The bottom of the curve, seen from above
The top of the curve, seen from above
questions.context: Water clings to the glass and climbs its sides, so its surface sags in the middle, and the volume is read at the bottom of that curve. Her eye must be level with it, because looking down from above lines the water up with the wrong mark.
questions.grade_note: Graduated cylinders are among TEKS 5.1D's glassware, and elementary lessons teach reading the bottom of the curve at eye level.

questions.question: A drop of pond water holds bacteria, living things far too small to see with the eye alone. A scientist wants a look at them. Which tool will show them to her?
choices: A microscope
A hand lens
A telescope
A magnifying mirror
questions.context: A school microscope makes things look from about 40 to hundreds of times bigger, enough to show bacteria. A hand lens magnifies only up to about 10 times and a magnifying mirror about 3 times, far too little for bacteria, and a telescope is built for things far away.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.1D names hand lenses and microscopes as the grade's tools for seeing small things, and choosing between them is part of using them.

questions.question: A student measures a pumpkin for the class science fair and writes four measurements in her notebook. Which one is the pumpkin's mass?
choices: 6 kilograms
8 litres
80 centimetres
15 degrees Celsius
questions.context: Kilograms and grams are units of mass, read from a balance. Litres and millilitres measure volume, centimetres and metres measure length (here, a tape around the pumpkin's middle), and degrees Celsius measure temperature, read from a thermometer.
questions.grade_note: 5th graders measure with metric tools (TEKS 5.1D), and NGSS 3-5 asks for accurate measurements, which means matching each quantity to its unit.

questions.question: A student needs the mass of a scoop of sand, but the sand has to sit in a paper cup on the balance. How does she find the mass of the sand alone?
questions.answer: Take away the mass of the empty cup
choices: Take away the mass of the empty cup
Add on the mass of the empty cup
Read the balance just as it stands
Take away the volume of the empty cup
questions.context: The balance finds the mass of the cup and the sand together, so the cup's own mass must come off the total: if the empty cup is 5 grams and both read 85 grams, the sand is 80 grams. Many digital scales do this with a tare button, pressed with the empty cup on them. A cup's volume is the space it fills, not its mass, so it cannot come off a reading in grams.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.1D gives 5th graders scales and glassware, and finding the mass of sand or water in a container on a balance means taking away the container's mass.

questions.question: Lena and her classmates test whether a bigger paper parachute falls more slowly than a smaller one. They hang the same load on both, drop each from the same height and time each fall with a stopwatch. Why do they keep the load and the height the same?
questions.answer: So only the size can cause a difference
choices: So only the size can cause a difference
So both parachutes fall at the same speed
So the result agrees with their prediction
So they need to drop each one only once
questions.context: In a fair test only one thing is changed, here the size, and everything else is kept the same, so any difference in the falling times must come from the size. Keeping the rest the same does not make the results match each other or anyone's guess, and the class should still drop each parachute several times.
questions.grade_note: Changing one variable and keeping the rest the same is the heart of 5th-grade fair testing (TEKS 5.1B; NGSS 3-5 planning investigations).

questions.question: A student drops a ball from 1 metre and uses a metre stick to measure how high it bounces. Her teacher asks her to make the very same drop three times. Why do scientists repeat a trial like this?
questions.answer: One drop alone might give an odd result
choices: One drop alone might give an odd result
Each new drop tests a different variable
A test only counts if it is done three times
The first drop is only ever for practice
questions.context: Small slips, such as letting go a little high or reading the stick at a slant, change each result a little, so a single drop may be off. Repeating the same drop and comparing or averaging the results gives a more trustworthy answer. There is nothing special about three, and every drop counts.
questions.grade_note: The grades 3-5 investigation practice asks students to plan fair tests with the number of trials considered, and 5th-grade labs repeat each trial.

questions.question: A boy predicts that his biggest magnet will pick up the most paper clips. He tests each of his magnets five times, and every time a small magnet picks up more clips than the big one. What should he do about his prediction?
questions.answer: Change his idea to fit the results
choices: Change his idea to fit the results
Keep his idea, since he was so sure
Call the whole test a failure
Test until the big magnet wins
questions.context: A prediction is an idea to be tested, and when careful, repeated results go against it, the honest move is to change the idea. The test did not fail: it showed that size is not all that matters, for a small neodymium magnet can pull harder than a much bigger magnet of a weaker kind.
questions.grade_note: 5th graders test predictions and use the evidence to explain (TEKS 5.1E, 5.3A), and NGSS 3-5 teaches that explanations change with new evidence.

questions.question: Four students each bring a question to the school science fair. Which question can a fair test answer?
questions.answer: Do bean plants grow taller in sun or shade?
choices: Do bean plants grow taller in sun or shade?
Is a rose a lovelier flower than a tulip?
Should every school plant a garden of its own?
Is gardening the best hobby for a family?
questions.context: Science answers only questions that evidence, such as measurements, can settle: beans can be grown in sun and in shade, with everything else kept the same, and their heights measured. Which flower is lovelier and which hobby is best are matters of taste, and what schools should do is a choice for people to make, so no test can settle them.
questions.grade_note: NGSS grades 3-5 teaches that science findings are limited to what evidence can answer, and TEKS 5.1A starts every investigation with a testable question.

questions.question: A student reads a thermometer outside every hour from dawn to dusk and writes the temperatures in a table. What should she draw to show how the temperature changes through the day?
choices: A line graph
A pie chart
A Venn diagram
A flow chart
questions.context: A line graph joins the hourly readings with lines, so the temperature's rises and falls through the day can be seen at a glance. A pie chart shows the parts of a whole, a Venn diagram shows what two groups share, and a flow chart shows the steps of a process in order.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.1F asks 5th graders to record data in tables, graphs, Venn diagrams and flow charts and to choose the right one.
